verifyNote: Written from GOC standards and College of Optometrists guidance. How the final clinical year is organised depends on your route: integrated MOptom programmes run their own clinical learning in practice under the GOC's 2021 Education and Training Requirements, while some students complete the College of Optometrists' Scheme for Registration. Always follow your own programme's handbook.

topics.title: How the final placement year works
topics.summary: The final clinical year turns a student into a safe, independent optometrist. You work with real patients in practice or hospital under the supervision of a registered optometrist, build up a record of patient episodes across a wide range of patients, and are assessed against the outcomes needed to join the GOC register. Your university (or the College, on the Scheme for Registration) sets the exact rules.

keyPoints.text: You must be registered with the GOC as a student optometrist throughout, and follow the GOC Standards for Optical Students.
A named supervisor (a registered optometrist) oversees your work and signs off your progress.
Supervision starts close (supervisor present or checking every patient) and becomes more distant as you show competence.
You build a portfolio: patient episodes, reflective entries, feedback and evidence against the required outcomes.
You need experience with a wide range of patients: children, older people, contact lens wearers, people with binocular vision problems, eye disease and low vision.
Final assessment leads to eligibility to register as a fully qualified optometrist.

examTraps.text: Thinking a supervisor's presence removes your own responsibility: you are accountable for your actions as a student.
Waiting until the end of the year to fill gaps in your patient log.
Treating reflection as box-ticking: assessors look for what you learned and changed.

diagram.description: A timeline across the final year: induction and close supervision → building patient episodes and reflections → interim review with supervisor/university → more independent practice and filling gaps → final assessment → GOC registration as an optometrist.

goDeeper.heading: Working with your supervisor
goDeeper.body: Agree early how you'll work: which patients you'll see, when they'll check, how you'll get feedback and how you'll raise concerns. Ask for direct observation regularly, not just sign-offs. If something worries you about a patient, stop and ask: safe practice always comes before speed. If the placement isn't working, use your university's (or the College's) support routes early.

goDeeper.heading: GOC Standards for Optical Students
goDeeper.body: As a student you must, among other things: listen to patients and put them first, communicate effectively, get valid consent, work within your competence, keep your knowledge up to date, keep accurate records, protect confidentiality, be honest and open when things go wrong, and raise concerns about patient safety. These continue into the Standards of Practice once you qualify.

goDeeper.heading: Old and new routes
goDeeper.body: Under the GOC's 2021 Education and Training Requirements, approved MOptom programmes integrate clinical learning in practice and the university assesses you. Students on older degree routes may instead complete the College of Optometrists' Scheme for Registration, with its own stages and final assessment. The aim is the same: safe, independent practice at the point of registration.

topics.title: Your patient log and reflective practice
topics.summary: Your patient log is the evidence that you've seen enough patients, of enough kinds, and handled them safely. Reflection turns that experience into learning: thinking about what happened, why, and what you'd do differently. Both are assessed, and both become habits you'll need for CPD throughout your career.

keyPoints.text: Log each patient episode as your programme requires: date, age band, what you did, findings, management and supervision level.
Never include identifiable patient details in your portfolio; anonymise everything.
Aim for breadth: different ages, refractive errors, binocular vision, contact lenses, low vision, eye disease and referrals.
Reflective models such as Gibbs' cycle (description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan) give structure.
Good reflection is specific and leads to action: what you'll do differently and how you'll check it worked.
Ask for written feedback after observed episodes and reflect on it.

examTraps.text: Writing reflections that only describe what happened.
Putting names, dates of birth or addresses in your log.
Logging lots of similar routine patients and missing whole categories.

diagram.description: Gibbs' reflective cycle drawn as a circle of six steps with arrows: Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusion → Action plan → back to Description.

goDeeper.heading: A good reflection
goDeeper.body: Description: 'I missed a small inferior retinal haemorrhage that my supervisor found.' Feelings: 'I felt embarrassed and worried.' Evaluation: 'The rest of the exam went well; my fundus view of the periphery was rushed.' Analysis: 'I was running late and skipped asking the patient to look down.' Conclusion: 'Time pressure led me to cut corners.' Action: 'I'll follow a set sequence of gaze positions every time and ask for help with time management.'

goDeeper.heading: Confidentiality in your portfolio
goDeeper.body: Use age bands rather than dates of birth, and no names, addresses, NHS numbers or unusual details that could identify someone. Keep your portfolio secure, follow your practice's data protection policy and never photograph records or screens with patient details on your own phone.

goDeeper.heading: From log to CPD
goDeeper.body: Once registered, the GOC's CPD scheme expects you to plan your learning, take part in activities across your scope, do peer review and reflect on your practice. Keeping a reflective log as a student makes this natural rather than a last-minute task.

topics.title: Running a full routine eye examination
topics.summary: By the end of the year you should run a complete eye examination safely and efficiently on your own: a focused history, vision and refraction, binocular vision, a full eye health check with any extra tests needed, and a clear explanation and plan for the patient. The skill is in tailoring the exam to each person while never missing the essentials.

keyPoints.text: History: reason for visit and symptoms, previous eye history, general health, medicines, allergies, family history, work, hobbies, driving and screen use.
Vision and refraction: unaided and habitual acuity, objective (retinoscopy or autorefraction) and subjective refraction, near and intermediate needs.
Binocular vision: cover test, motility, near point of convergence and other tests guided by symptoms.
Eye health: external eye and anterior segment (slit lamp), pupils, fundus examination, with IOP and visual fields as indicated by age, risk or findings.
Management: explain findings, prescribe or not, advise, refer if needed, set a recall interval and record everything.
In the NHS: check eligibility for a NHS sight test (GOS in England; in Scotland NHS eye examinations are free for everyone).

examTraps.text: Doing every test on every patient without thinking, and running out of time for what matters.
Prescribing a small change that won't help: 'not prescribing' can be the right choice.
Forgetting to explain results and next steps clearly to the patient.

diagram.description: A flow chart of a routine eye examination: History → Vision → Objective refraction → Subjective refraction → Binocular vision → Anterior eye → Pupils → Posterior eye → Additional tests (IOP, fields, OCT) → Management, advice, recall → Records.

goDeeper.heading: Tailoring the examination
goDeeper.body: Let the history lead. A headache at the computer points you to near and intermediate refraction and binocular vision. A family history of glaucoma means IOP, disc assessment and fields. Flashes and floaters mean a dilated peripheral retinal examination. Diabetes means a careful look for retinopathy and checking screening attendance. Keep a core routine, then add what the patient needs.

goDeeper.heading: Deciding whether to prescribe
goDeeper.body: Compare the new result with the old prescription and the patient's symptoms. Small changes in an asymptomatic patient often don't need new glasses. Consider adaptation (big cylinder or axis changes), occupation, driving vision standards and binocular status. Explain your reasoning; the patient's informed choice matters.

goDeeper.heading: Recall intervals
goDeeper.body: Recall is based on clinical need: commonly every two years for adults, and more often for children, older people, people with diabetes or a family history of glaucoma, and anyone being monitored. Check local NHS rules for how often a funded sight test is allowed. Always advise patients to come back sooner if their vision or eyes change.

checklist.title: Routine eye examination (outline)
steps: Confirm identity, consent and NHS eligibility; review previous records.
Take a focused history: symptoms, eye and general health, medicines, allergies, family history, lifestyle and driving.
Measure unaided and habitual vision at distance and near.
Perform objective then subjective refraction, including near and intermediate needs.
Assess binocular vision (cover test, motility, NPC and others as indicated).
Examine external eye and anterior segment, and pupils.
Examine the fundus (dilate if indicated), with IOP, fields and imaging as indicated.
Explain findings, prescribe or advise, refer if needed and agree a recall interval.
Complete clear, contemporaneous records and any NHS paperwork.

topics.title: Referral letters and communicating with other professionals
topics.summary: Knowing when to refer, how urgently, and how to write a clear referral is one of the most important skills an optometrist has. Good referrals give the receiving clinician everything they need, at the right urgency, through the right local pathway, and keep the patient informed and safe in the meantime.

keyPoints.text: Decide urgency: emergency (same day), urgent (within about a week) or routine, using College of Optometrists Clinical Management Guidelines and local protocols.
Use local pathways where they exist: community urgent eye care services, glaucoma repeat measures, cataract direct referral, and so on.
A referral should include patient details, reason and urgency, relevant history, findings (with both eyes' acuities, IOP, fields as relevant), medicines, allergies and your contact details.
Emergency referrals should be made by phone (and followed up in writing), not just by letter.
Tell the patient why you're referring, how urgent it is, what to expect and what to do if things get worse; give them a copy where appropriate.
Record the referral, the urgency and the advice given.

examTraps.text: Sending an emergency referral by post or email only.
Writing 'please see' with no findings or reason.
Forgetting to give safety-net advice to the patient.

diagram.description: Three columns: Emergency (same day, phone first: e.g. acute angle closure, retinal detachment, CRAO, giant cell arteritis, chemical injury), Urgent (within about a week: e.g. suspected wet AMD per local fast-track, very high IOP without symptoms per guidance), Routine (e.g. cataract affecting daily life, stable glaucoma suspect via pathway).

goDeeper.heading: What a good referral letter looks like
goDeeper.body: Start with the urgency and the question: 'Urgent referral: suspected wet AMD, right eye.' Then: symptoms and duration; relevant history; findings for both eyes (VA, refraction if relevant, IOP with method and time, disc/macula description, fields, OCT if done); medicines and allergies; what you've told the patient; your name, GOC number and contact details. Keep it clear, factual and easy to scan.

goDeeper.heading: Structured communication
goDeeper.body: For phone referrals, a structure such as SBAR helps: Situation (who you are, who the patient is, what's happening), Background (history), Assessment (your findings and what you think it is) and Recommendation (what you want: for example 'please see today'). Write down who you spoke to, when and what was agreed.

goDeeper.heading: Safety-netting
goDeeper.body: Tell the patient exactly what to do if symptoms change: for example 'If you notice a curtain coming across your vision, go to the eye emergency department today.' Make sure they know how and when they'll hear about their appointment, and what to do if they don't. Record this advice.

cases.scenario: A 74-year-old reports that straight lines on her door frame look wavy in her right eye for the past week. VA R 6/18 (was 6/9), L 6/9. You see a small haemorrhage and raised area at the right macula.
cases.question: How would you refer, and what would you tell her?
cases.modelAnswer: Suspected wet (neovascular) AMD: refer urgently via the local fast-track pathway so she's seen quickly (often within about two weeks, sooner if possible), including VA, symptoms, duration, macular findings and OCT if available. Explain why the referral is urgent and that treatment works best early, check she knows how she'll be contacted, and tell her to get in touch if her vision worsens further or she hears nothing. Give an Amsler grid for the other eye and record everything.

topics.title: Records, consent and safeguarding in practice
topics.summary: Every patient contact must be recorded accurately, every examination needs valid consent, and every optometrist has a duty to protect children and adults at risk. These professional basics are tested throughout your placement and are central to the GOC standards.

keyPoints.text: Records must be clear, accurate, contemporaneous, dated, signed or attributable, and kept securely for the required period.
Valid consent must be informed, voluntary and given by someone with capacity; it can be withdrawn at any time.
Adults are presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005 in England and Wales); if they lack it, act in their best interests.
Young people under 16 may consent if they understand fully (Gillick competence).
Safeguarding: recognise signs of abuse or neglect, follow your practice's safeguarding policy, and report concerns to the safeguarding lead or local authority; emergencies go to the police.
Confidentiality can be breached only in specific circumstances, such as risk of serious harm to the patient or others, or when required by law.

examTraps.text: Writing 'normal' without saying what was checked.
Assuming someone lacks capacity because of a diagnosis such as dementia: capacity is decision-specific.
Investigating a safeguarding concern yourself instead of reporting it.

diagram.description: A flow chart: Concern about a child or adult → Is anyone in immediate danger? Yes → call 999. No → record what you saw and heard (facts, words used) → speak to the practice safeguarding lead → referral to local authority (children's or adult social care) as advised → record actions.

goDeeper.heading: Good records
goDeeper.body: Record what was done and found, not just conclusions: 'Pupils: PERRLA, no RAPD' or 'Fundus: discs C/D 0.3 healthy rims, maculae flat, vessels normal, periphery flat (dilated, Volk 90D)'. Include advice given, drugs used (name, strength, batch, time), referrals and recall. Never alter records after the event without clearly marking and dating the addition.

goDeeper.heading: Consent and capacity
goDeeper.body: Explain what you'll do, why, any risks (for example dilation effects) and alternatives. A person has capacity for a decision if they can understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a decision. If they can't, a decision must be made in their best interests, involving people close to them where possible. Record how consent was obtained.

goDeeper.heading: Recognising safeguarding concerns
goDeeper.body: Signs can include unexplained injuries (including around the eyes), a child brought repeatedly with injuries, neglected glasses or missed appointments for a child with a serious condition, an adult who seems frightened of a carer, or someone else answering every question for them. You don't need proof to raise a concern: record facts and pass it on through the right route.

topics.title: Final assessments, GOC registration and your first job
topics.summary: Passing your final assessments makes you eligible to join the GOC register as an optometrist. From then on you must follow the GOC Standards of Practice, keep up CPD, hold professional indemnity insurance and, to do NHS work in England, join the ophthalmic performers list. Planning these steps early makes the move into your first job smoother.

keyPoints.text: Final assessment format depends on your route (university assessment within an integrated MOptom, or the College's final assessment on the Scheme for Registration).
Once eligible, apply to the GOC to join the register; you can't practise as an optometrist until you're registered.
You must have professional indemnity insurance (often through a professional body or employer).
The GOC Standards of Practice for Optometrists and Dispensing Opticians replace the student standards.
CPD: the GOC requires continuing professional development across each three-year cycle, including peer review and reflection; check the current requirements.
NHS work in England needs inclusion on the ophthalmic performers list; other UK nations have their own lists.

examTraps.text: Starting work as an optometrist before your GOC registration is confirmed.
Leaving CPD until the end of the cycle.
Assuming your employer's insurance covers all work you do privately or elsewhere.

diagram.description: Steps from final assessment to first job: Pass final assessment → Apply to GOC register → Professional indemnity insurance → Performers list (for NHS work) → Start work → CPD cycle with peer review and reflection.

goDeeper.heading: Preparing for final assessments
goDeeper.body: Know the format early (practical stations, viva, case-based assessment or portfolio review). Practise full routines under time pressure, rehearse explaining findings to patients, and revise emergency recognition and referral thoroughly; safety-critical errors matter most. Use your patient log to spot weaker areas and get observed practice on them.

goDeeper.heading: Your first job
goDeeper.body: Look for support: a structured induction, access to an experienced colleague, reasonable testing times at first and protected time for learning. Ask about equipment (OCT, fields), referral pathways and enhanced services. Joining a professional body (for example the College of Optometrists or the Association of Optometrists) gives access to guidance, CPD and advice.

goDeeper.heading: Fitness to practise
goDeeper.body: The GOC can investigate concerns about a registrant's conduct, competence or health. Most problems can be prevented by working within your competence, keeping good records, communicating clearly, being honest when things go wrong and asking for help early. Tell the GOC about any cautions or convictions as required.
